A.explanation: Point X is ahead of the motion, so wavefronts bunch together there and observed frequency cannot decrease, and water wave speed is set by the medium.

B.explanation: Wave speed staying the same is correct, but the bunched wavefronts ahead of the moving insect mean more waves per second arrive at X, so frequency does not decrease.

C.explanation: Frequency increasing is correct for X ahead of the source, but wave speed in the water is unchanged by source motion.

D.explanation: Wavefronts are closer together ahead of the insect so observed wavelength $\lambda$ falls and observed $f = v/\lambda$ rises, while $v$ is fixed by the water.

hints: Look at diagram 2 at point X on the right: the circular wavefronts are crowded closer together ahead of the insect moving to the right than in diagram 1.
Connect wavefront spacing to observed wavelength at X, and recall that observed frequency is $f = v/\lambda$ for the waves arriving there.
Ask what sets the water wave speed $v$ - the source motion or the properties of the water - to decide if $v$ or $f$ changes at X.
walkthrough: In diagram 1 the source is stationary so wavefronts are equally spaced in all directions. In diagram 2 the insect moves right toward X, so each new wave is emitted from a position closer to X.
This piles up the wavefronts ahead of the source, as seen by the reduced spacing on the right side in diagram 2. So the apparent wavelength $\lambda_{obs}$ at X is smaller.
The speed $v$ of surface water waves is determined by the medium, not by the speed of the source, so $v$ at X stays the same.
For waves arriving at X, $v = f_{obs} \lambda_{obs}$ with constant $v$. A smaller $\lambda_{obs}$ must give a larger observed frequency $f_{obs}$.
More wavefronts per second therefore sweep past X because the source is chasing its own waves forward. This is the Doppler effect for a source moving toward the observer.
Frequency increases and wave speed stays the same. This is option D.
